atoms.statement: A total function $f(x,\vec{z})$ is regular if for every sequence of natural numbers $\vec{z}$ there is an $x$ such that $f(x,\vec{z}) = 0$, and the regular functions are exactly those to which unbounded search can be applied and still yield a total function.

evidence.text: Say a total function f (x, ⃗z) is regular if for every sequence of natural numbers ⃗z, there is an x such that f (x, ⃗z) = 0.
In other words, the regular functions are exactly those functions to which one can apply unbounded search, and end up with a total function.

atoms.statement: Although the definition of general recursive functions (which restricts unbounded search to regular functions) differs from the definition of recursive functions (total partial recursive functions, which may use partial recursive functions along the way), the set of general recursive functions and the set of recursive functions are one and the same.

evidence.text: The difference between Definition 2.30 and Definition 2.27 is that in the latter one is allowed to use partial recursive functions along the way; the only requirement is that the function you end up with at the end is total.
But, fortunately, the difference is illusory; though the definitions are different, the set of general recursive functions and the set of recursive functions are one and the same.

atoms.statement: The set of general recursive functions, defined as the smallest set of functions containing zero, successor, and projections and closed under composition, primitive recursion, and unbounded search applied only to regular functions, is the same set as the set of recursive functions (the total partial recursive functions), even though the general recursive definition looks less general because the latter definition allows partial recursive functions to be used along the way.

evidence.text: Definition 2.30. atoms.statement: In a model $\mathfrak{M}$ of PA, the block of a non-standard element $x$ is the set of those $y \in |\mathfrak{M}|$ such that $x \oplus n = y$ or $y \oplus n = x$ for some standard $n$, and this block has no least and no greatest element.

evidence.text: If one wishes to study planar graphs that are not triangulations, it is often convenient to work with double circle packings, which enjoy similar rigidity properties to usual circle packings, but for the larger class of polyhedral planar graphs.

atoms.statement: Among the eight mammalian P2Y receptors, P2Y1, P2Y11, P2Y12 and P2Y13 are activated by adenosine nucleotides.

evidence.text: The eight mammalian P2Y receptors are activated by distinct nucleotides: P2Y1, P2Y11, P2Y12 and P2Y13 are activated by adenosine‐­nucleotides; P2Y2, P2Y4 can be activated by both adenosine and uridine nucleotides, with some species‐­specific differences; P2Y6 is mainly activated by UDP; P2Y14 is preferentially activated by sugar‐­uracil nucleotides.

atoms.statement: Based on their G protein coupling, P2Y receptors can be divided into two subfamilies: P2Y1, P2Y2, P2Y4, P2Y6 and P2Y11 receptors couple via Gq proteins, whereas P2Y12, P2Y13 and P2Y14 receptors signal primarily through Gi proteins.

evidence.text: Based on their G protein coupling P2Y receptors can be divided into two subfamilies: P2Y1, P2Y2, P2Y4, P2Y6 and P2Y11 receptors couple via Gq proteins to stimulate phospholipase C followed by increases in inositol phosphates and mobilization of Ca2+ from intracellular stores.
In contrast, P2Y12, P2Y13, and P2Y14 receptors signal primarily through activation of Gi proteins and inhibition of adenylate cyclase activity or control of ion channel activity [2958].

atoms.statement: P2Y receptors are activated by the endogenous ligands ATP, ADP, UTP, UDP, and UDP-sugars.

atoms.statement: Many ligands described as 'antagonists' of cAMP accumulation, for example carvedilol and bucindolol, weakly activate MAP kinase pathways and thus display biased agonism.

evidence.text: Many ‘antagonists’ of cAMP accumulation, for example carvedilol and bucindolol, weakly activate MAP kinase pathways [130, 741, 835, 836, 2485, 2486] and thus display biased agonism.

atoms.statement: Agonists display biased signalling at the β2-adrenoceptor via Gs or via arrestins.

evidence.text: Agonists also display biased signalling at the β2‐­adrenoceptor via Gs or arrestins [677].

atoms.statement: Several α1A-adrenoceptor agonists display ligand-directed signalling bias relative to noradrenaline.

evidence.text: Several α1A‐­adrenoceptor agonists display ligand directed signalling bias relative to noradrenaline [739] although some bias appears to relate to off‐­target activity [569] .

atoms.statement: At the β2-adrenoceptor, compounds displaying β-arrestin-biased signalling have a greater effect on the conformation of transmembrane helix 7 (TM7), whereas full agonists for Gs coupling promote movement of TM5 and TM6.

evidence.text: Compounds displaying β‐arrestin‐­biased signalling at the β2‐­adrenoceptor have a greater effect on the conformation of TM7, whereas full agonists for Gs coupling promote movement of TM5 and TM6 [1713].
